case_info.scenario: A healthy 25-year-old female presented with an 8-month history of a painful right mandibular lesion (Figure 1A). The patient reported progressive persistent pain and enlargement of the lesion since it was first noticed. She denied any facial trauma history and had no sensory deficits in the inferior alveolar nerve distribution or signs of infection such as purulent discharge, foul taste, warmth, or erythema of the overlying skin. She had multiple prior emergency department encounters for this lesion, and maxillofacial computed tomography revealed a multiloculated radiolucent lesion situated below the inferior alveolar nerve at the right mandibular angle (Figure 1B). On clinical examination, there was firm, tender external swelling of the right gonial angle along the inferior border. Intraoral findings were unremarkable, with no drainage or evident expansion into the retromolar trigone. An incisional biopsy was performed via a transoral approach. The intralesional content appeared to be dark brown and spongy. A portion of the tissue was sent for frozen section analysis, which revealed the presence of multinucleated giant cells and spindle cells but was nondiagnostic. A fluorescence in situ hybridization study was subsequently performed, confirming a positiveUSP6gene rearrangement.

B, Coronal view of maxillofacial computed tomography (CT) showing a multiloculated lesion at the right mandibular angle. The lesion is expansile in nature and located inferior to inferior alveolar nerve. It demonstrates cortical invasion involving both the buccal and lingual aspects.
case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Intraoral findings were unremarkable, with no drainage or evident expansion into the retromolar trigone. An incisional biopsy was performed via a transoral approach. case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

{

case_info.scenario: A healthy 25-year-old female presented with an 8-month history of a painful right mandibular lesion (Figure 1A). The patient reported progressive persistent pain and enlargement of the lesion since it was first noticed. She denied any facial trauma history and had no sensory deficits in the inferior alveolar nerve distribution or signs of infection such as purulent discharge, foul taste, warmth, or erythema of the overlying skin. She had multiple prior emergency department encounters for this lesion, and maxillofacial computed tomography revealed a multiloculated radiolucent lesion situated below the inferior alveolar nerve at the right mandibular angle (Figure 1B). On clinical examination, there was firm, tender external swelling of the right gonial angle along the inferior border. Intraoral findings were unremarkable, with no drainage or evident expansion into the retromolar trigone. An incisional biopsy was performed via a transoral approach. The intralesional content appeared to be dark brown and spongy. A portion of the tissue was sent for frozen section analysis, which revealed the presence of multinucleated giant cells and spindle cells but was nondiagnostic. A fluorescence in situ hybridization study was subsequently performed, confirming a positiveUSP6gene rearrangement.

B, Coronal view of maxillofacial computed tomography (CT) showing a multiloculated lesion at the right mandibular angle. case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.
